title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
intro: A matrix moves vectors around: it stretches, turns, flips and squashes them. But almost every matrix has a few special directions that it does not turn at all, only stretches. Those are its eigenvectors, and the stretch factors are its eigenvalues. Knowing them tells you what the matrix does, what happens when you apply it again and again, and how a system built on it behaves over time.

blocks.text: Take the matrix below and apply it to a vector $v$. In general $Av$ points somewhere new: the matrix has turned $v$ as well as stretched it. Now look for a direction where that does not happen, where $Av$ lands on the same line as $v$:

Such a $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the number $\lambda$ (lambda) is its eigenvalue. If $\lambda = 3$, the matrix triples every vector along that line; if $\lambda = -1$ it flips them; if $\lambda = 0$ it squashes them to nothing. For the symmetric matrix

the vector $(1, 1)$ goes to $(3, 3)$, three times itself, and $(1, -1)$ goes to $(1, -1)$, unchanged. So the eigenvalues are 3 and 1. Every other vector is a mix of those two, and $A$ triples one part and keeps the other, which is why it seems to turn them.

The first viewer shows a 2×2 matrix at work. The dashed circle is every vector of length 1; the solid ellipse is where $A$ sends them. The probe $v$ and its image $Av$ are the dark and the red arrow, and the two grey arrows are the columns $Ae_1$ and $Ae_2$. The eigen-directions are the dashed coloured lines, each labelled with its $\lambda$, with a thick arrow for $\lambda v$. On the right, the top graph splits $Av$ into a part along $v$ and a part sideways as $v$ turns from 0° to 180°: the sideways part is zero exactly at an eigen-direction, and there the along part is $\lambda$. The bottom graph is the characteristic polynomial, whose roots are the eigenvalues. Press Next step ▶ to walk through it in eight steps.

params.label: Matrix A
options: your own (use the sliders a, b, c, d)

items: Matrix A picks one of thirteen matrices: stretches, a symmetric and a non-symmetric one, a reflection, a projection, a shear, rotations and spirals, the Fibonacci matrix and a Markov chain. A fourteenth option, your own, uses the four sliders a, b, c and d as the entries of $A$; moving a slider switches to it.
Direction of v turns the probe; Sweep v turns it for you. Watch the two arrows line up as $v$ crosses a dashed line.
Powers shown, k, draws the directions of $v, Av, A^2v, \ldots, A^kv$ as numbered dots on the circle. For most matrices they swing towards the eigen-direction with the largest $|\lambda|$.
The readout below the steps prints the matrix, its trace and determinant, the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and $Av$ for the current probe.

blocks.text: The default matrix is $[[2, 1], [1, 2]]$ with $v$ at 20°. $Av$ points further round than $v$. Drag Direction of v to 45° and $Av$ lies on the blue line, three times as long as $v$: $\lambda = 3$. At 135° it lies on the teal line and is exactly $v$: $\lambda = 1$.

The second viewer does the same for a 3×3 matrix in space. The grey globe is the unit sphere, and the green surface is its image: an ellipsoid, or something flat if the matrix squashes a direction. Dashed lines are the real eigen-directions, a blue disc marks a whole plane of eigenvectors, and an amber disc marks the plane that a complex pair of eigenvalues turns. Below are the characteristic polynomial, a cubic, and the numbers. Drag the view to turn it.

blocks.text: The default matrix is symmetric, so its three eigen-directions are perpendicular and are exactly the axes of the green ellipsoid. Its eigenvalues are $2 + \sqrt{2} \approx 3.414$, $2$ and $2 - \sqrt{2} \approx 0.586$, the half-lengths of those axes. Choose rotation by 60° about the z-axis and only the z-axis survives as an eigen-direction, with $\lambda = 1$; the amber disc is the plane being turned.

items: Directions a Matrix Keeps (#/math/eigenvalues/invariant-directions): a matrix as a map of the plane, and the special directions it only stretches.
Finding Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/math/eigenvalues/finding-eigenvalues): the characteristic polynomial, worked for 2×2 and 3×3 matrices, and solving for the vectors.
Diagonalisation and Powers (#/math/eigenvalues/diagonalisation): changing to the eigenbasis, A = PDP⁻¹, and fast powers, with the Fibonacci numbers in closed form.
Symmetric Matrices and the Spectral Theorem (#/math/eigenvalues/symmetric-matrices): real eigenvalues, perpendicular eigenvectors, ellipses, and quadratic forms.
Complex Eigenvalues and Rotation (#/math/eigenvalues/complex-eigenvalues): what a complex pair means: turning and scaling in a plane, in 2D and 3D.
Repeated Eigenvalues and Defective Matrices (#/math/eigenvalues/repeated-eigenvalues): algebraic and geometric multiplicity, shears, and Jordan blocks.
Power Iteration and Markov Chains (#/math/eigenvalues/power-iteration): why repeated multiplication finds the dominant eigenvector, steady states, and PageRank.
Eigenvalues in Practice (#/math/eigenvalues/applications): differential equations and stability, vibration modes, principal components, and how computers find eigenvalues.
A Gallery of Matrices (#/math/eigenvalues/gallery): every matrix in the two viewers, and what each one teaches.
Eigenvalue Tables (#/math/eigenvalues/tables): reference tables: matrix types and their eigenvalues, rules for transformed matrices, and the 2×2 and 3×3 formulas.

blocks.text: Vectors, matrix-vector multiplication and the determinant of a 2×2 matrix. The quantum shelf's Linear Algebra for Quantum Mechanics (#/quantum/foundations/linear-algebra) covers these, and its page Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/quantum/foundations/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors) meets the same ideas with complex Hermitian matrices, the kind quantum mechanics uses. Here the matrices are real and the pictures are geometric. Later pages link to The Laplace Transform (#/math/laplace-transform) (poles and stability) and to Markov Chains (#/probability/processes/markov-chains) on the probability shelf.
